item.title: AI can turn security fixes into working exploits before users receive an update (16 minute read)
item.description: GLM 5.3 can identify and exploit vulnerabilities in recent versions of the Mozilla Firefox browser using security fixes that have been published but not yet shipped to users. Open-source projects are particularly vulnerable to this kind of attack as their code is publicly available. This threat vector will likely worsen as open-weight cyber capabilities continue to improve.

item.title: The surprising leadership dynamics in agent swarms (17 minute read)
item.description: Agent swarms are groups of agents that work together to accomplish a task. Researchers created an experiment in which eight agents from four different models worked together to resolve simulated outages to understand how agents organize themselves in a swarm without a designated leader. They discovered two factors that could influence an agent's potential leadership: the agent's underlying models, and the order in which their name was listed in a prompt. This suggests that even seemingly minor details in how an agent swarm is configured can affect how agents coordinate.

item.title: The sleep framework: A new way for LLMs to retain knowledge in continual learning (11 minute read)

item.title: Knowing How Is Not Knowing What (14 minute read)
item.description: RL training environments need to integrate a domain's unwritten rules into the reward so that agents can only get the task right by knowing them or going and finding them. Environments should be built as one world exposed through several surfaces. This allows you to pose the same task at different difficulties by changing the surface, and agents get a chance to learn when to switch. The reward also reads the world, so agents that go through different surfaces get the same outcome score if they reach the same authorized result.

item.title: Bitter Lessoned in Automated Theorem Proving (13 minute read)

Models will one-shot superior work for pennies in the very near future.

item.title: OpenAI nears up to $30 billion funding round at $1.25 trillion valuation led by UAE investors (3 minute read)
item.description: OpenAI is closing in on a funding round that could value it at more than $1 trillion. Investors from the United Arab Emirates are leading the round. The round is being positioned as an opportunistic bridge ahead of a potential IPO. OpenAI is aiming to secure signatures by the end of next week, but the final size of the round is still being determined.

item.title: Introducing 1Password for Agents (7 minute read)
item.description: 1Password introduced a platform that lets AI agents authenticate to websites without accessing users' passwords directly. Agents can request credentials from a user's vault, and once approved, 1Password autofills them into the destination site while keeping the credentials hidden from the agent.

item.title: WorldTUI: I trained a 360M model to pretend to be a terminal (18 minute read)
item.description: WorldTUI is a 360-million-parameter model fine-tuned to act as a terminal. The model predicts how the screen will change for every key press, and there is no shell or file system behind it. WorldTUI can create files, run vim and tmux, play snake, and usually remember commands. It can repair mistakes and decode screen rows in parallel. A browser demo is available.

item.title: How the US and China Could Verifiably Slow AI (29 minute read)
item.description: A unilateral US pause will fail because rivals would catch up within about a year, so any slowdown needs a treaty that catches defection early. This post surveys how one could govern compute through remote sensing, on-site inspections, and hardware mechanisms like chip licensing and location verification.

item.title: How Researchers Tested OpenAI's Internal Agent Monitoring (6 minute read)
item.description: METR and Redwood Research conducted a three-week security assessment with access to OpenAI's internal infrastructure, identifying vulnerabilities that could allow AI agents to evade monitoring, bypass sandbox restrictions, or conceal actions.

item.title: Does Flapping Airplanes Mean Short Timelines and Hard Treaty Enforcement? (7 minute read)
item.description: Flapping Airplanes' potential valuation jump from $1.5B to $5B may reflect investor hype rather than verified technical progress. Breakthroughs in sample-efficient AI could accelerate superintelligence timelines and make compute-based treaty enforcement harder.

item.title: Claude's Text Output Now Carries an Invisible Watermark (9 minute read)
item.description: Anthropic's latest Claude models embed a SynthID-Text-based watermark in all text output to comply with the EU AI Act. It works by nudging choices among near-equivalent words, adds no hidden characters or tokens, and carries no information about the user.

item.title: A Novel Self-Distillation Method (7 minute read)
item.description: Perplexity's JOLT is a self-distillation method that jointly trains a model as both teacher and student, adapting feedback to the student's capabilities. It improved performance and training efficiency across mathematical reasoning, coding, and agentic tasks.

item.title: How we deploy Trillion-parameter frontier models on Cerebras (6 minute read)
item.description: A single Cerebras WSE-3T wafer has 44 GB of on-chip memory. Trillion-parameter frontier models need terabytes of memory for their weights alone. This post explains how the company splits a large frontier model across multiple WSE-3T wafers. It covers how models are filled into on-chip memory, how models are mapped across multiple chips, and how Cerebras handles a high number of concurrent requests.

item.title: NVIDIA's Video Generation with Matching 3D Motion (4 minute read)
item.description: NVIDIA has introduced Joints, Camera, Action! (JCA), a system that generates videos and synchronized 3D motion for arbitrary character rigs from text prompts. It supports scene-aware motion, keyframe-based control, and bidirectional conversion between video and rig animation.

item.title: An Interview with OpenAI's Richard Ho on Why Jalapeño Is a Groundbreaking AI Chip (22 minute read)
item.description: OpenAI's Jalapeño AI inference chip outperforms its rivals in performance per watt. It is likely the most promising chip program in the latest wave of non-GPU AI chips. This post contains highlights from a conversation with one of the top engineers in the AI and chip industry. The interview is packed with technical details and insights on where chip design and memory technology are going.

item.title: What happened to the missing Gemini 3.5 Pro model that never shipped? (1 minute read)
item.description: Google had both Flash and Pro versions of the 3.5 series. However, there were gaps in the model's agentic capabilities, particularly around coding. The team felt the fastest way to climb that hill was to use Flash, as the smaller model allowed for more iterative loops. By the time the team had improved Flash's abilities, Argon pre-training was done.

item.description: TorchTPU is an open-source PyTorch backend designed to make running and migrating models to Google's TPUs easier. It supports training and inference through optimized eager execution, torch.compile integration, and native hardware acceleration.

item.title: llm-d (Website)
item.description: llm-d is a Kubernetes-native stack for distributed LLM inference. It runs vLLM, SGLang, and more across clusters, turning single-node engines into production-grade serving on local hardware. llm-d provides tested deployment recipes for common production patterns that are adaptable starting points across models, hardware, and workloads. It runs production LLM inference across GPUs, TPUs, XPUs, CPUs, and emerging NPUs with consistent performance patterns, so teams can deploy once and scale anywhere with predictable cost and behavior.

item.title: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash: Large-Scale Inference Deployment (15 minute read)
item.description: DeepInfer combines distributed inference, caching, load balancing, and speculative decoding to improve efficiency. DeepSeek processes 155 trillion tokens daily per cluster and earns $38 in revenue per GPU-hour while open-sourcing much of its inference framework.

item.title: Making every harness durable (7 minute read)
item.description: Vercel's durable-harness allows agent harnesses to run durably in the cloud out-of-the-box. It allows users to run Pi, OpenCode, Codex, and Claude Code durably on Vercel or self-hosted on their own Postgres instance. durable-harness ensures that sessions survive crashes mid-turn and keep running even if the browser disconnects. Turns that lose function partway through continue from the log on a new one without manual retry and without repeating what already finished.

item.title: Building Laminar: Ramp's Managed Agents Platform (14 minute read)
item.description: Laminar is an in-house agent harness for Ramp's agentic products. It features secure conversation history storage, session compaction, standard interfaces for tool calling, message queuing and steering, subagents, multiplayer chat support, observability tooling, and much more. The first version of Laminar was built in six weeks with a small team of obsessive, experienced engineers who worked with and steered the agents. Its code was generated entirely by agents using the most powerful models available at the time. While building in-house has become cheaper, Ramp still needs good engineers to be on-call, keep the platform healthy, and figure out what product teams actually need and how it fits into the bigger picture.
